design_detail: PET study with the VMAT2 ligand (+)[11C]dihydrotetrabenazine ((+)[11C]DTBZ), whose binding at tracer doses rises when vesicular dopamine is low. Cross-sectional comparison at a first scan (mean 2.6 days after last use) between 28 people who used methamphetamine, 9 people who used cocaine and 22 controls, plus a short prospective follow-up: a second scan about a week later in those who stayed abstinent (17 methamphetamine, 8 cocaine, 9 controls). Binding potential (BPND) by simplified reference-tissue model with occipital reference, in limbic, associative and sensorimotor striatum and whole striatum, with a voxelwise analysis.
can_establish: That striatal (+)[11C]DTBZ binding was higher in people actively using methamphetamine, scanned a few days after last use, than in controls or in people who used cocaine, that it tracked recency and frequency of recent use, and that in the subgroup who stayed abstinent about ten days it was no longer distinguishable from controls.
cannot_establish: That vesicular dopamine itself was measured (binding is an indirect, competition-based index and VMAT2 protein could also change), that use caused the difference (no pre-use scan; groups differ in education, IQ, depression, smoking and cannabis), that the follow-up shows recovery in users generally (only those who stayed abstinent were rescanned, and they already had lower binding at scan 1), or that users were cognitively impaired relative to controls (group comparisons appear only in the supplement and are described as slight).

sample.recruitment: Self-referred in response to a web advertisement; non-treatment-seeking, actively using participants; all compensated for their time. Data from 12 of the 22 controls were taken from the authors' earlier 2008 study; all drug users were new recruits (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 19–45, no significant medical condition or head trauma. Controls: no current or past DSM-IV Axis I disorder (SCID), no abuse or dependence in the past 12 months except nicotine, negative urine GC-MS and scalp-hair toxicology except cannabis. Users: DSM-IV abuse or dependence on their respective drug, with positive urine and hair toxicology (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.demographics: Table 1. Age: controls 28.6 (SD 5.8), methamphetamine 26.6 (5.7), cocaine 31.2 (7.7). Men: 12, 12 and 3. Education (years): 16.8 (2.6) vs 13.1 (2.7), p<0.001. IQ (Shipley-2): 111.6 (12.9) vs 101.4 (12.2), p=0.03. Beck Depression Inventory: 1.1 (1.5) vs 14.6 (10.9), p<0.001. Smokers: 4 of 22 controls vs 24 of 28 methamphetamine and 7 of 9 cocaine (p<0.001); cigarettes per day 0.5 (1.3) vs 9.5 (5.6). Cannabis at least monthly: 3 vs 18 (p=0.02). Alcohol drinks per week 0.6 (1.0) vs 4.1 (7.3), p=0.14. Ethnic composition differed (p=0.01). Several control values are compiled from 10 longitudinal controls plus the earlier study's controls (Table 1, footnote a).
sample.attrition: Of 28 people who used methamphetamine, 17 were rescanned; 7 did not stay abstinent and were therefore not rescanned (described as choosing methamphetamine over the study honorarium); 4 dropped out or were lost to excessive head movement. Controls: 9 of 22 rescanned; cocaine: 8 of 9. Those who relapsed had higher binding at scan 1, so the completers are a selected subgroup (Results › PET Results; Table 3 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Actively using, non-treatment-seeking volunteers recruited online and paid, compared with controls who were better educated, scored higher on an IQ screen, were far less often smokers and had minimal depressive symptoms. Rescanning only the abstinent subgroup selects on the outcome's own predictor.

exposure.measurement: DSM-IV diagnosis plus self-report (Severity of Dependence Scale, DAST-20) with biological verification: urine and blood toxicology at each scan and scalp-hair analysis covering roughly the preceding 4–5 months. Plasma methamphetamine measured before scan 1 (Materials and Methods › Subjects; Table 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported, Table 2: methamphetamine group, 6.6 (SD 5.7) years of use; 4.3 (2.4) days per week in the past month; 0.35 (0.30) g per day; 49.9 (24.1) days used in the past 90; routes 14 smoking, 6 nasal, 4 smoking and nasal, 2 oral, 2 intravenous. Cocaine group: 13.7 (8.5) years, 1.9 (1.9) days per week, 0.64 (0.30) g per day. Reported as study-sample characteristics.
exposure.polysubstance: Extensive. Hair toxicology of the 28 methamphetamine participants also showed cocaine or benzoylecgonine in 17 (60%), MDMA/MDA in 6, opioids in 4 and THC in 6; cocaine was detected in urine in only one case during the study. Most were tobacco smokers and 18 used cannabis at least monthly. Analyses were adjusted for cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, current cannabis use and depressive symptoms, but not for other stimulant exposure, education or IQ (Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Table 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Scan 1: mean 2.6 days (SD 2.0, range 1–7) since last use, verified by self-report plus urine and blood toxicology. Scan 2: mean 9.9 days (SD 2.3) in the methamphetamine group; participants who used in between were not rescanned (Table 2; Materials and Methods).

comparison.controls: 22 healthy volunteers without current or past Axis I disorder or recent substance use disorder other than nicotine; 9 of them were rescanned. A cocaine-using group (n=9) served as a stimulant comparison.
comparison.matching: Matched on age and sex; not matched on education, IQ, depressive symptoms, ethnicity, smoking or cannabis use, all of which differed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan or cognitive baseline; current IQ screen and education differed between groups and were not adjusted for.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls had negative urine and hair toxicology except cannabis; 3 used cannabis at least monthly and 4 smoked tobacco.

outcomes.instruments: (+)[11C]DTBZ PET on an HRRT camera, about 10 mCi, 60-minute acquisition, BPND by simplified reference-tissue model with occipital reference; automated regions for limbic, associative and sensorimotor striatum and whole striatum; voxelwise SPM8 analysis. Questionnaires and a cognitive battery at each session: Hopkins Verbal Learning Test, Delay Discounting Task, Continuous Performance Task, Amphetamine Withdrawal Questionnaire, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Beck Depression Inventory (Materials and Methods; Results).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors state the tracer competes with vesicular dopamine for the VMAT2 site, so higher binding is read as less stored dopamine; they note VMAT2 protein itself might change and that residual methamphetamine could compete with the tracer at scan 1 (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Cognitive tests are standard instruments; normative comparison is not reported in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Low vesicular dopamine was operationalized as higher (+)[11C]DTBZ binding; recovery as binding not differing from controls at the second scan. Cognitive impairment in the abstract rests on within-group correlations between binding and test scores, not on a group comparison (Results › correlations paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Group contrasts: repeated-measures ANOVA followed by least-significant-difference t-tests with Bonferroni correction for planned comparisons. Voxelwise: p<0.01 with family-wise correction. Correlations: no correction stated; about 15 correlations are reported at a 0.05 threshold across four striatal regions and several behavioural measures (Materials and Methods › Statistical Analyses; Results).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; regions were placed by an automated method, which limits operator influence.

analysis.effect_sizes: Scan 1 (Table 3; means with SD): whole striatum BPND 2.41 (0.34) in controls, 2.55 (0.30) in cocaine users, 3.09 (0.71) in methamphetamine users, i.e. +28% vs controls (p<0.0001) and +21% vs cocaine users (p=0.040). By region vs controls: associative +31% (p<0.0001), limbic +24% (p=0.010), sensorimotor +26% (p<0.0001). Group effect F(2,56)=9.581, p<0.0001; ROI × group interaction F(1.485, 83.146)=5.077, p=0.001. Cocaine users did not differ from controls (+6%, p=1.0). Editors' calculation from Table 3 (Hedges' g, pooled SD, approximate 95% CI): methamphetamine vs controls whole striatum g=1.24 (0.63 to 1.85), associative g=1.38 (0.76 to 2.00), sensorimotor g=1.17 (0.56 to 1.77), limbic g=0.88 (0.29 to 1.47). Adjusting for cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, cannabis and depressive symptoms left the group effect significant (F(2,55)=5.723, p=0.006; F(2,43)=5.036, p=0.011; F(2,43)=5.723, p=0.006). Scan 2 (17 methamphetamine, 8 cocaine, 9 controls): whole striatum 2.54 (0.39) vs 2.46 (0.34) in controls, all contrasts p=1.0, F(2,48)=0.288, p=0.751. Within the 17 who stayed abstinent, binding fell about 11% from scan 1 (p=0.055), with individual changes from −34% to +29% and 6 of 17 increasing. People who relapsed before scan 2 (n=7) had 17% higher scan-1 binding than those who stayed abstinent (n=17) (ANCOVA with days abstinent, p=0.035); the abstainers' scan-1 binding was already closer to controls (limbic p=0.472, whole striatum p=0.031). Correlations within the methamphetamine group at scan 1 (n=28): frequency of recent use r=0.68 (p<0.0001), cumulative amount in the past month r=0.48 (p=0.009), days abstinent r=−0.49 in associative striatum (p=0.008), plasma methamphetamine r=0.5 (p=0.008). Participants who had used about 24 hours before the scan (n=10) had binding 45–52% above controls; those abstinent 2–7 days (n=18) were 13–20% lower than them. Scan-1 binding predicted scan-2 binding (limbic r=0.76, p<0.001; whole striatum r=0.54, p=0.026; associative r=0.49, p=0.045). Binding correlated with verbal recall r=−0.43 (p=0.03), cued recall r=−0.46 (p=0.02), recognition r=−0.46 (p=0.01), delay discounting r=0.43 (p=0.03), processing speed r=0.43 (p=0.03), withdrawal symptoms r=0.37 (p=0.051) and sleepiness r=0.44 (p=0.011).
analysis.covariates: Cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, current cannabis use, depressive symptoms (each in a separate adjusted ANOVA); days abstinent in the relapser-versus-abstainer comparison; baseline binding in the partial correlations of change. Education, IQ, ethnicity and concurrent cocaine exposure were not adjusted for.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cognitive and behavioural comparisons between users and controls are placed in supplementary tables and summarized in one sentence as slight deficits, while the abstract reports correlations with cognitive impairment. The relapsers' course after scan 1 is unobserved by design.
analysis.power: Not reported. The follow-up contrast rests on 17 users and 9 rescanned controls; the within-group change (11%) did not reach the 0.05 threshold.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Striatal (+)[11C]DTBZ binding was about 28% above control levels a few days after last use, scaling with how recently and how often methamphetamine had been used, and indistinguishable from controls in the subgroup who managed about ten days of abstinence; the within-person fall was 11% (p=0.055) and a third of that subgroup rose rather than fell. Users differed from controls in education, IQ, depressive symptoms, smoking and cannabis use, and 60% had hair evidence of cocaine exposure.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and abstract describe rapid recovery of vesicular dopamine levels and say the elevated binding correlated with cognitive impairment and withdrawal symptoms. Vesicular dopamine is inferred, not measured; the authors say so in the discussion and note VMAT2 protein may itself change. Recovery rests on rescanning only those who stayed abstinent, who already had lower binding at scan 1, against 9 rescanned controls, with no retested comparison for practice or regression effects. Cognitive impairment is supported by within-group correlations; the paper's own group comparison, reported only in the supplement, is summarized as showing no marked impairment. The discussion of levodopa as dopamine substitution is framed cautiously as needing a safety trial first, and notes the hazard of giving it while the drug is still present.

timeline.event: The authors' earlier cross-sectional PET study reported raised VMAT2 binding in early abstinence (Boileau et al., 2008); 12 of its controls are reused here.
A PET study reported about 10% lower VMAT2 binding in users abstinent much longer (Johanson et al., 2006, as cited); direction opposite to the early-abstinence finding.
Review citing this study as evidence against substantial dopamine neurone loss, with binding raised in the first days and normal by 7–15 days
Meta-analysis listing VMAT2 findings in methamphetamine users as inconsistent across abstinence phases (Ashok et al., 2017; appraised in this batch).

replication.where_it_stands: Raised VMAT2 tracer binding in the first days of abstinence has now been reported twice by the same laboratory, with partly shared controls, and no independent replication was cited. Whether binding falls below normal at longer abstinence, and whether any of it reflects vesicular dopamine rather than transporter number, remains open.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA25096 to S.J.K. (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest (Funding and Disclosure).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and University of Toronto. The same group produced the post-mortem findings this study sets out to corroborate and the 2008 PET study it extends, and co-authored the Kish et al. (2017) review that cites it. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A study that rescans everyone, including those who resume use, with a retested control group over the same interval, measures VMAT2 with a method that does not compete with endogenous dopamine alongside (+)[11C]DTBZ, and reports the cognitive battery against controls and norms rather than only as within-group correlations.

key_findings.finding: At a mean of 2.6 days after last use, whole-striatum (+)[11C]DTBZ binding was 28% higher in 28 people who used methamphetamine than in 22 controls (BPND 3.09, SD 0.71, vs 2.41, SD 0.34; p<0.0001); 9 people who used cocaine did not differ from controls (+6%, p=1.0).
key_findings.locator: Results › MA users have greater binding during early abstinence; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Regional differences from controls at scan 1: associative striatum +31% (p<0.0001), sensorimotor +26% (p<0.0001), limbic +24% (p=0.010). Group effect F(2,56)=9.581, p<0.0001; ROI × group F(1.485, 83.146)=5.077, p=0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › first paragraph of PET Results; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from Table 3: standardized differences (Hedges' g) between methamphetamine users and controls at scan 1 of about 1.24 whole striatum (95% CI 0.63 to 1.85), 1.38 associative, 1.17 sensorimotor and 0.88 limbic.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation with pooled SD and large-sample interval; group SDs are unequal (0.71 vs 0.34), so the interval is approximate.

key_findings.finding: Adjusting separately for cigarettes per day, weekly alcohol, cannabis use and depressive symptoms did not remove the group difference (F(2,55)=5.723, p=0.006; F(2,43)=5.036, p=0.011; F(2,43)=5.723, p=0.006).
key_findings.locator: Results › first paragraph of PET Results
key_findings.note: Two of the three adjusted analyses use 43 error degrees of freedom, implying about 12 participants dropped from those models; this is not explained.

key_findings.finding: At the second scan (mean 9.9 days abstinent) the 17 who stayed abstinent did not differ from 9 rescanned controls in any region (whole striatum 2.54, SD 0.39, vs 2.46, SD 0.34; all p=1.0).
Within those 17, binding fell about 11% from scan 1 (p=0.055), with individual changes ranging from −34% to +29% and 6 of 17 increasing.
key_findings.note: The change over time was not significant at the paper's own 0.05 threshold.

key_findings.finding: The 7 participants who did not stay abstinent had 17% higher scan-1 binding than the 17 who did (p=0.035, adjusted for days abstinent) and were never rescanned; the abstainers' scan-1 binding was already much closer to controls (limbic p=0.472).
key_findings.locator: Results › first paragraph of PET Results; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Binding tracked recency and amount of use: frequency of recent use r=0.68 (p<0.0001), amount in the past month r=0.48 (p=0.009), days abstinent r=−0.49 (p=0.008), plasma methamphetamine r=0.50 (p=0.008); those who had used about 24 hours before the scan (n=10) were 45–52% above controls.

Within the 28 users, higher binding correlated with poorer verbal recall (r=−0.43), cued recall (r=−0.46), recognition (r=−0.46), steeper delay discounting (r=0.43), slower reaction time (r=0.43), more withdrawal symptoms (r=0.37, p=0.051) and more daytime sleepiness (r=0.44).
Compared with controls the users showed no marked cognitive or behavioural impairment, only slight deficits; those comparisons are reported in supplementary tables, not in the main text.
key_findings.note: Supplementary Tables 1 and 2 are .doc downloads and were not opened, so the size and direction of the group differences could not be checked.

key_findings.finding: The authors state they cannot exclude that VMAT2 protein itself changed, or that residual methamphetamine competed with the tracer at scan 1, and that it remains unknown whether low stored dopamine means low synaptic dopamine.

reporting_issues.issue: The second-scan analysis is reported as F(2,48)=0.288 although the three rescanned groups total 34 people (17, 8 and 9); for three groups this implies 51 participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the degrees of freedom or the stated group sizes are wrong; the test of normalization cannot be reconstructed as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 0.35 g per day and 49.9 days of use in the past 90 but an amount per month of 1.57 g; those three numbers are not mutually consistent (0.35 g on about 17 days a month would be roughly 6 g).
reporting_issues.consequence: The monthly exposure variable, which is used in a correlation with binding, may measure something other than monthly total.

reporting_issues.issue: The same correlation coefficient of −0.46 in the same group of 28 is given p=0.02 for cued recall and p=0.01 for recognition; r=0.44 is given p=0.011 while r=0.43 is given p=0.03.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the n varies between tests (missing data not stated) or some p-values are misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the three covariate-adjusted analyses use error degrees of freedom of 43, against 55 in the first and 56 in the unadjusted model, without explanation; the same F value (5.723) appears in both the cigarettes model (df 55) and the cannabis-plus-depression model (df 43).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › first paragraph of PET Results)
reporting_issues.consequence: Suggests a copying error in one of the adjusted results, and that 12 or more participants were lost from the adjusted models.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 heads the control column with two sample sizes (n=10 and n=22) and a footnote says some control values combine 10 longitudinal controls with controls from the authors' earlier study; which rows use which n is not marked.
reporting_issues.consequence: The control demographics cannot be matched to the control group actually scanned at each time point; 12 of the 22 controls were scanned for a different study.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 2 legend reports cluster significance as corrected p greater than 0.0001 and uses a correction abbreviation that matches neither the family-wise correction stated in the Methods nor a standard false-discovery label.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Figure 2 legend; Materials and Methods › image analysis)
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical, but the voxelwise correction actually applied cannot be verified from the legend.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 17 abstainers and 7 relapsers at scan 1, which with the 4 further non-completers accounts for 28, but the group row for scan 1 pools all 28 including the 4 whose subgroup is never characterized.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 4 excluded from both subgroups are not described, so the subgroup contrast is not exhaustive.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states binding correlated with cognitive impairment, while the Results state the users did not show marked impairment relative to controls.
reporting_issues.consequence: The word impairment in the abstract is supported only by within-group variation, not by a deficit against controls.

domains.note: Groups differ in education, IQ, depressive symptoms, ethnicity, smoking and cannabis; adjustment covered smoking, alcohol, cannabis and depression but not education, IQ or the 60% with hair evidence of cocaine exposure.
Diagnosis plus urine, blood and hair toxicology, with plasma methamphetamine at scan 1; amounts self-reported and internally inconsistent in Table 2.
Paid, non-treatment-seeking volunteers recruited by web advertisement against better-educated controls, 12 of whom came from an earlier study.
Abstinence between scans was participant-managed and verified; those who used were excluded from the follow-up rather than analysed.
Follow-up was obtained only from completers (17 of 28), and non-completion was directly related to the outcome, since those who relapsed had the highest binding.
Objective PET with automated regions, but the outcome is an indirect index: binding depends on vesicular dopamine, on VMAT2 number, and potentially on residual drug.

Cognitive group comparisons are confined to the supplement while correlations appear in the abstract; about 15 uncorrected correlations are reported, with p-values that do not all match their coefficients.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The cross-sectional difference is large, dose- and recency-related and survives several adjustments, so something about recent methamphetamine use is clearly reflected in the tracer signal. The recovery conclusion is much weaker: it rests on completers selected by the very behaviour that tracked the outcome, on a within-group change that did not reach significance, and on 9 rescanned controls. The cognitive conclusion is not supported by a group comparison in the main text.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4748442 (all sections, Tables 1–3 as text, figure legends; Figures 1–3 are images of scatter plots and a statistical map; Supplementary Tables 1 and 2, which hold the cognitive and behavioural group comparisons, are .doc downloads and were not opened)
